Q: What is JavaScript's highest integer value that a number can go to without losing precision? A:

Many earlier answers have shown 9007199254740992 === 9007199254740992 + 1 is true to verify that 9,007,199,254,740,991 is the maximum and safe integer.

But what if we keep doing accumulation:

input: 9007199254740992 + 1  output: 9007199254740992  // expected: 9007199254740993
input: 9007199254740992 + 2  output: 9007199254740994  // expected: 9007199254740994
input: 9007199254740992 + 3  output: 9007199254740996  // expected: 9007199254740995
input: 9007199254740992 + 4  output: 9007199254740996  // expected: 9007199254740996

We can see that among numbers greater than 9,007,199,254,740,992, only even numbers are representable.

It's an entry to explain how the double-precision 64-bit binary format works. Let's see how 9,007,199,254,740,992 be held (represented) by using this binary format.

Using a brief version to demonstrate it from 4,503,599,627,370,496:

  1 . 0000 ---- 0000  *  2^52            =>  1  0000 ---- 0000.  
     |-- 52 bits --|    |exponent part|        |-- 52 bits --|

On the left side of the arrow, we have bit value 1, and an adjacent radix point. By consuming the exponent part on the left, the radix point is moved 52 steps to the right. The radix point ends up at the end, and we get 4503599627370496 in pure binary.

Now let's keep incrementing the fraction part with 1 until all the bits are set to 1, which equals 9,007,199,254,740,991 in decimal.

  1 . 0000 ---- 0000  *  2^52  =>  1  0000 ---- 0000.  
                       (+1)
  1 . 0000 ---- 0001  *  2^52  =>  1  0000 ---- 0001.  
                       (+1)
  1 . 0000 ---- 0010  *  2^52  =>  1  0000 ---- 0010.  
                       (+1)
                        . 
                        .
                        .
  1 . 1111 ---- 1111  *  2^52  =>  1  1111 ---- 1111.

Because the 64-bit double-precision format strictly allots 52 bits for the fraction part, no more bits are available if we add another 1, so what we can do is setting all bits back to 0, and manipulate the exponent part:

  ┏━━▶ This bit is implicit and persistent.
  ┃        
  1 . 1111 ---- 1111  *  2^52      =>  1  1111 ---- 1111. 
     |-- 52 bits --|                     |-- 52 bits --|

                          (+1)

  1 . 0000 ---- 0000  *  2^52 * 2  =>  1  0000 ---- 0000. * 2  
     |-- 52 bits --|                     |-- 52 bits --|
                                      (By consuming the 2^52, radix
                                       point has no way to go, but
                                       there is still one 2 left in
                                       exponent part)
  =>  1 . 0000 ---- 0000  *  2^53 
         |-- 52 bits --|

Now we get the 9,007,199,254,740,992, and for the numbers greater than it, the format can only handle increments of 2 because every increment of 1 on the fraction part ends up being multiplied by the left 2 in the exponent part. That's why double-precision 64-bit binary format cannot hold odd numbers when the number is greater than 9,007,199,254,740,992:

                            (consume 2^52 to move radix point to the end)
  1 . 0000 ---- 0001  *  2^53  =>  1  0000 ---- 0001.  *  2
     |-- 52 bits --|                 |-- 52 bits --|

Following this pattern, when the number gets greater than 9,007,199,254,740,992 * 2 = 18,014,398,509,481,984 only 4 times the fraction can be held:

input: 18014398509481984 + 1  output: 18014398509481984  // expected: 18014398509481985
input: 18014398509481984 + 2  output: 18014398509481984  // expected: 18014398509481986
input: 18014398509481984 + 3  output: 18014398509481984  // expected: 18014398509481987
input: 18014398509481984 + 4  output: 18014398509481988  // expected: 18014398509481988

How about numbers between [ 2 251 799 813 685 248, 4 503 599 627 370 496 )?

 1 . 0000 ---- 0001  *  2^51  =>  1 0000 ---- 000.1
     |-- 52 bits --|                |-- 52 bits  --|

The value 0.1 in binary is exactly 2^-1 (=1/2) (=0.5) So when the number is less than 4,503,599,627,370,496 (2^52), there is one bit available to represent the 1/2 times of the integer:

input: 4503599627370495.5   output: 4503599627370495.5  
input: 4503599627370495.75  output: 4503599627370495.5

Less than 2,251,799,813,685,248 (2^51)

input: 2251799813685246.75   output: 2251799813685246.8  // expected: 2251799813685246.75 
input: 2251799813685246.25   output: 2251799813685246.2  // expected: 2251799813685246.25 
input: 2251799813685246.5    output: 2251799813685246.5
/**
   Please note that if you try this yourself and, say, log 
   these numbers to the console, they will get rounded. JavaScript
   rounds if the number of digits exceed 17. The value 
   is internally held correctly:
*/
            
input: 2251799813685246.25.toString(2) 
output: "111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111110.01"
input: 2251799813685246.75.toString(2) 
output: "111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111110.11"
input: 2251799813685246.78.toString(2)   
output: "111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111110.11"

And what is the available range of exponent part? 11 bits allotted for it by the format.

Q: Sharing Jupyter Notebook/Lab output with not technical people A:

The Mercury is an open-source tool that converts Jupyter Notebook into shareable web applications. The main trick is that it hides the code cells and only keep outputs. The next nice thing that it has a collection of GUI widgets that can be added to the notebook. GUI widgets in Mercury are reactive, when you change widget value it automatically re-execute code cells below for you. It makes Mercury easy way to built web apps from Jupyter Notebooks and share with non-technical users.

You can read more about newest (v3) Mercury release and here is Mercury documentation website.

Q: What scope is advised for Hibernate StatelessSession? A:

The recommended lifecycle for a Hibernate StatelessSession when using applications executing high-throughput message processing (like Apache Kafka consumers) or batch processes where standard HTTP request scopes do not exist, register a custom transaction scope.

Use CustomScopeConfigurer to define a bean with the custom scope @Scope("transaction"). So, it means when you make a database transaction the bean is created, and it no longer available when the transaction ends.

Q: Ai is the replacer of Web developer A:

You should spend your time on what you like doing.

If you like web development, go for it.

But you're going to need to learn to use AI. With the help of AI your work as a web developer can be sped up by a factor of 5x to 100x (depending on how well you can tame AI to do your work). For junior devs, AI can help with solving simple, concrete problems ("how do I do X", or "what's the best way to do X") - all perfectly solvable by a human after spending a day or two - AI can solve it in seconds. For senior devs, AI can speed up implementation ("here are my goals/tasks - implement them"). For architects, AI can do almost everything ("here are my goals, constraints - make a spec, plan tasks and implement").

Q: Under what conditions does the host memory used to create an OpenCL buffer get updated? A:

The simple way to ensure that the data on the host is up-to-date is to use a single command queue and do a blocking read buffer API call. If there are no subsequent enqueued commands that modify the buffer, the data on the host is up-to date once the blocking read completes. Not until after an explicit read buffer API call has finished executing are the changes guaranteed to be on the host side. Without the explicit read buffer API call, one can't say anything certain about that buffer, so accessing it via the host should be avoided. I don't know for sure about the API internals, but I suspect it could cause race conditions to do so.

More complicated applications may make use of multiple command queues and/or non-blocking read/write operations. In this case, care must be taken to ensure that the buffer is not being modified during the read buffer API call or while it is accessed by the host. One can make use of other blocking operations, events, or sync. points like clFinish() to achieve this.
